The reproductive biology of the Gray four-eyed opossum (Philander opossum) reflects a life-history strategy adapted to relatively stable tropical environments, where resources are predictably available throughout the year. Females typically give birth to a litter of 5 pups [N_R_i = a litter of 5 pups] and can produce up to 3 litters each year [F_R_i = up to 3 litters each year], a pattern observed at a core body temperature of 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C], which is characteristic of active didelphids during their foraging periods. This combination of moderate litter size and repeated reproductive events yields a high annual fecundity compared to many larger mammals. Gestation is remarkably brief, lasting only 13.5 days [tg = 13.5 days] under the same thermal conditions, a figure consistent with the extremely short placentation period known among marsupials at a temperature of 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C]. Viviparous birth produces neonates weighing a miniscule 0.2 grams [Wwb = 0.2 grams], underscoring the altricial nature of the newborn pups, which immediately embark on a journey to the teat within the maternal pouch.

Following parturition, the neonatal individuals begin an intense period of growth fueled entirely by maternal milk during the suckling stage. Weaning, defined as the cessation of lactation and the onset of nutritional independence, occurs at 82 days after birth [tx = 82 days after birth] at 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C]. At this point, the young have attained a wet weight of approximately 110 grams [Wwx = approximately 110 grams] upon transitioning to solid food, a substantial increase from their birth mass. Captive records indicate a broader range for weaning mass, generally falling between 100 and 120 grams [Wwx = between 100 and 120 grams], likely reflecting variation in maternal provisioning and litter size. This weaning age is relatively extended for a small marsupial, suggesting that the slow pace of suckling development is an adaptation that allows the altricial neonates to complete critical organogenesis while attached to the teat.

Sexual maturity in females is not reached until well after the juvenile stage has been completed, a pattern common among didelphids that balances the energetic demands of growth against the onset of reproductive effort. Under the stable thermal regime of 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C], the time since birth at puberty for females is 450 days since birth [tp = 450 days since birth], meaning that a young female born early in the year will typically not experience her first oestrus until the beginning of the following breeding season. This delayed maturation, equivalent to approximately 15 months, allows for extensive foraging and mass accumulation. By this age, individuals are approaching their asymptotic body dimensions, although full size may take additional months. Female puberty at this age is a critical life-history transition, marking the onset of gametogenesis and the potential for the individual to contribute to the next generation.

The species displays a pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with adults ultimately attaining different maximum body masses. Field studies indicate that the ultimate wet weight for females is 1200 grams [Wwi = 1200 grams], while males are considerably larger, achieving an ultimate wet weight of 1500 grams [Wwi = 1500 grams]. This appreciable difference in mass is likely linked to male-male competition for access to receptive females, a common dynamic in solitary didelphid species where larger body size confers an advantage in agonistic encounters. Juveniles grow steadily after weaning, and captive data show that at one year of age, individuals generally reach a wet weight of around 740 grams , with a recorded captive range of 673 to 800 grams (673-800 grams) . This sub-adult mass indicates that growth continues well into the second year of life.

Longevity under natural conditions is moderate for a mammal of this body size, with most individuals succumbing to predation or disease before reaching extreme ages. The maximum lifespan recorded at 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C] in captivity is 4.4 years [am = 4.4 years], a figure that reflects the relatively fast-paced life history of small-bodied marsupials compared to eutherians of similar mass. In the wild, senescence is rarely observed, and the oldest documented individuals in the field likely do not exceed three years, given the high extrinsic mortality pressures. This short maximum lifespan, coupled with early maturation and multiple litters per year, positions Philander opossum as a classic r-selected species within the constraints of its marsupial reproductive physiology. The data collectively illustrate a life history geared toward rapid replacement rather than prolonged survival.
